posts.title: Everyone Is Talking About AI. But Are Businesses Actually Getting Value From It?
posts.body:
Everyone is talking about AI, and companies are pouring real money into it. The harder question is whether that money is actually producing results.

Research the Wall Street Journal highlighted recently points to a familiar problem: AI budgets keep growing, but plenty of leaders still can't clearly say what return they're getting for that spend. Honestly, that shouldn't surprise anyone. It's easy for a company to decide "we need AI." It's much harder to answer the follow-up question — what exactly are we going to use it for, and how will we know it worked?

AI shouldn't be adopted just because everyone else seems to be doing it. A business should start with the problem it's trying to solve, not the tool. Maybe that's automating repetitive admin work. Maybe it's improving customer support response times. Maybe it's helping the IT team catch security threats earlier. Maybe it's making sense of data that's been sitting unused for years. Whatever it is, the technology should follow the business problem, not the other way around.

Governance is the other piece companies tend to skip. Who's actually allowed to use AI tools at your company? What information are employees allowed to put into them? Which tools are approved, and who's keeping an eye on how they're used? What's the plan if an AI system gets something wrong? These used to feel like theoretical questions. They aren't anymore — AI has moved out of the experimentation phase and into everyday operations for a lot of businesses, including ones that never had a real policy conversation about it.

If there's one lesson I keep coming back to, it's this: don't measure your AI strategy by how many AI tools your company has adopted. Measure it by the problems those tools have actually solved. The companies that get that right tend to get far more value out of AI than the ones just chasing whatever's trending.
